catalog_quote: 18.3 Factors Determining Stress. Several factors help to determine which syllable or morpheme will be stressed. There is no doubt that the predominant factor is phoneme strength. This includes the phonemes' relationship to one another in syllables, and the relative weight of syllables in keeping or shifting stress. Another factor is what kinds of suffixes are involved. There are ones that are always stressed, stressed ones that can become unstressed and ones with slight stress. There are some that are unstressable, and some unstressed which have stress foisted on them. And there are the catalyst suffixes which force stress on others. ... The final factor is how many and which suffixes are being added to the verb. The more suffixes that are added, the further away from it moves the stress. ... I am eager to know if there are other languages whose stress rules rely largely on vowel streng…
sweep_summary: this search of works with stress in the title for Karkar-Yuri (kark1258, Pauwasi) turned up a single stress-titled item, Price 1981 'Determining stress in Karkar' (SIL archive 31140), which is already the catalog's deciding source and already held held by the project (copied with scanned and page images into and logged). Read on the page images: sec. 18.2 (ms pp.51-52) gives the default position (stem-initial; last stem syllable under suffixation; else first stressable suffix) and sec. 18.3 (ms p.55) the 'phoneme strength' predominance quoted verbatim in the catalog, so the item confirms the 'segmental' coding; nothing supersedes it. The SIL archive record (www.sil.org/resources/archives/31140, HTTP 200, Subject: Stress, Draft posted 'as is', 55 pp., created 1981) was. No other stress/accent/prosody title exists for this language in Glottolog, Semantic Scholar or Crossref; the only list of works to obtain rival, Price 1987 orthography paper, could not be reached (old sil.org URL 404, no archived copy at the Internet Archive per archive.org/the Internet Archive/available, web.archive.org could not be reached by automated download, pnglanguages.sil.org and www.sil.org search pages not reachable by automated download)

new_statements.quote: I had discovered Karkar-Yuri was stress-timed, not syllable-timed, with shorter words slower and longer words faster. Though an earlier investigator had thought it was a tonal language, I discovered it to be one with remarkably varied intonation. [p.57] [...] To a native speaker of Karkar and those outsiders who have absorbed the system, writing stress is unnecessary. The stress system is so intricate that it was necessary to deal with it in a separate paper (Price 1981) [p.63] [...] As more and more suffixes are added to a verb, the stress shifts further towards the end of the word. If a verb root with one or two suffixes still retains stress, the suffixes stay with it. [pp.73-74]

new_statements.locator: sec. 0-1, p.57 (PDF p.1); sec. 1.3, p.63 (PDF p.7); sec. 2.12 'Word length', pp.73-74 (PDF pp.17-18), example (35)
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Price 1981 statement (it cites that paper as the stress account); adds that the language is stress-timed and non-tonal (an earlier investigator's tonal analysis is rejected), that stress is not written except in the dictionary, and restates the rightward shift of stress under suffixation. The catalog's open_url (sil.org/pacific/png/pubs/0000260/..) is dead (404, no archived copy at the Internet Archive); the paper was found as SIL-PNG archive entry 23747 and downloaded from the Internet Archive copy of the SIL reapdata PDF (direct sil.org is an automated-access block-403).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated in this orthography paper; it characterises Karkar-Yuri as stress-timed and not tonal, calls the stress system 'unique' and 'so intricate' that it is treated in Price 1981, says stress is not written in the practical orthography, and (sec. 2.12) that stress moves rightward onto suffixes as more suffixes are added to a verb, with example (35): ao'kwap 'to go', ao'kwapea 'go and..', aokwap 'riaka, aokwap na'nampono 'I will go'.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; example (35a) ao'kwap shows a disyllabic stem stressed on its second syllable, i.e. the initial default is not absolute
new_statements.identity_note: All eight works describe Karkar-Yuri [yuj] (Price's 'Karkar'), the Pauwasi language of the Green River area, West Sepik/Sandaun Province, PNG, bordering Anggor; the OPD calls it 'Karkar-Yuri Isolate' within a 'Trans New Guinea Phylum' label. Not to be confused with the Karkar Island languages (Takia, Waskia). Price 1981 marks one plural form '(dialect)' but names no dialects; no dialect-specific stress claims appear anywhere.

new_statements.quote: Much work has been done on the phonological aspects of the Stress System in this language by Dorothy Price (1984). This describes the functioning of stress on the phoneme level. However, although the significance of stress as a focus factor has not been fully explored, it does appear that there are semantic implications in the placing of stress. Stress on the initial syllable of a word indicates that DESTINATION or GOAL is in FOCUS and stress on the final syllable indicates that the SOURCE is in FOCUS, e.g 'korop ko'rop 'come'

new_statements.rule_in_words: A discourse-prominence study, not a phonology; its one page on stress says stress position within a word can shift for focus: initial stress ('korop) signals that the destination/goal is in focus, final stress (ko'rop) that the source is in focus; the handwritten addition on the same page notes that in Ono 'korop 'namp ono 'I have just come' stress on both words is initial and focuses the destination. No fixed-position label fits this pragmatically mobile placement; the author defers the phonological account to Price.
new_statements.exceptions: the focus-driven alternation itself is presented as tentative ('has not been fully explored')

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the first syllable of the stem, overridden by 'phoneme strength': front and back vowels attract stress over central vowels, heavy syllables (labial/velar codas, Cw onsets, glottal stop, final -r?) attract stress, and word balance matters; when suffixes are added stress moves to the last stem syllable and, if it cannot shift within the stem, to the first stressable suffix; some suffixes are inherently stressed, unstressable, or 'catalyst' suffixes that force stress onto others.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not treated as such; ms p.50 says syllables of an initially stressed word are more even in loudness and length
new_statements.exceptions: sec. 1.1 (ms p.1): 'There appears to be contrastive stress on a few words' (erér/é'rér etc.); sec. 18.1 lists conflicting pairs (tu'kup vs 'tekep, 'korop vs to'rok, ka'kap vs 'kakap) and concludes stress 'can be predicted' only 'in most cases'; the author says the usual cross-linguistic stress rules 'do not apply at all to Karkar'

new_statements.quote: Stress is perceived as greater length and intensity, and is usually lower-pitched, except clause-finally, where it is high pitch. (The expected position for stress on words is on the first syllable. This can be contradicted only by the operation of vowel hierarchy and heavy-syllable and word balance rules. As mentioned above, the stressed word-initial syllable is only a little longer and louder than the following ones, with the third syllable taking secondary stress in 3-syllable words. However if it occurs on another syllable, stress is clearly louder and longer. Word stress is subordinate to phrase stress, and the greatest stress will be found within the final clause of the sentence.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, six years after Price 1981: the clearest one-paragraph statement of the initial default plus vowel-hierarchy/weight overrides; adds the phonetic correlates (length, intensity, usually lower pitch, high clause-finally), secondary stress on the third syllable, and the phrase-stress hierarchy. Recommended as the quotable summary for the site alongside the 1981 sec. 18.2 sentences.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Expected stress on the first syllable; this is overridden only by the vowel hierarchy (front unrounded > back rounded > central), syllable weight (CVVCC > CVCC > CVC > CV; long consonants such as Cw and glottal stop add weight) and word balance, e.g. 'grasshopper' vs pa'mbwae? 'banana species' where a final glottal stop pulls stress to the heavy second syllable; sec. 6.3 adds that reduplicated plurals keep initial stress and delay the shift under suffixation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: third syllable carries secondary stress in three-syllable words; word stress is subordinate to phrase stress, greatest in the final clause of the sentence
new_statements.exceptions: placement contradicted by vowel-hierarchy and heavy-syllable/word-balance rules; initial stress only slightly longer and louder than following syllables

Syllable weight and word balance and types of suffixes also affect the stress. Unusual contrastive intonation occurs on one word-final grammatical particle. [p.3] [...] Stress < ' > is written only in the dictionary. [p.4]

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts another on placement. Price 1981 (sec. 18.2), Price 1987 pluralization ms (sec. 2.2) and the 2004 OPD all describe an initial default overridden by a vowel-quality hierarchy (front/back 'strong' vowels over central 'weak' ones), syllable weight and suffix morphology; Price 1987 (orthography) restates the rightward shift under suffixation and adds that the language is stress-timed and not tonal, explicitly rejecting an unnamed earlier investigator's tonal analysis. The only tension is of type rather than placement: Rigden 1985 (ms p.49) presents initial vs final stress on the same verb ('korop vs ko'rop) as a focus device, and Price 1981 (ms p.1) notes 'contrastive stress on a few words' and (sec. 18.1) that stress is predictable only 'in most cases'; both fit a system whose default is initial but whose surface position is neither fixed nor fully rule-governed, which is why no fixed-position label applies and the catalog's segmental/vowel-strength coding remains the best fit.
